title: T1055.009 — Process Injection - Proc Memory
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Process Injection - Proc Memory with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Eight step simulation of a Proc Memory injection. An attacker with a web shell on a Linux server reads /proc/pid/maps, opens /proc/pid/mem with write access, injects code into a daemon, and the daemon beacons to command and control. A SOC panel on the right collects audit, eBPF and netflow evidence, and the final step shows containment.

steps.title: Foothold
steps.caption: The attacker exploits a web application and lands on the Linux server through a web shell. A web shell is a hidden script that turns a browser into a command prompt.
steps.defender: a suspicious child process appears under the web service process tree, away from normal deployment jobs.

steps.title: Target selection
steps.caption: The attacker lists processes under /proc, the Linux process file system, and picks a long-running daemon called metrics-agent, PID 812. A daemon is a background service, and a PID is a process identifier.
steps.defender: a short-lived shell reads many process status files in a row.

steps.title: Memory map
steps.caption: The attacker reads /proc/812/maps. This file lists the memory ranges of the daemon, so the attacker can choose a writable address, such as an unused gap, for the new code.
steps.defender: a web-spawned shell reads the memory map of an unrelated service. That is a strong reconnaissance signal.

steps.title: Open the memory file
steps.caption: The attacker opens /proc/812/mem with read and write access, the O_RDWR flag. The kernel allows it because both processes run under the same user ID.
steps.defender: auditd records an openat on /proc/812/mem with write flags and a success result.

steps.title: Write the code
steps.caption: The attacker moves the file position with lseek to the chosen address and writes a small piece of position-independent code, which runs at any address.
steps.defender: a write syscall succeeds on the /proc/812/mem file descriptor. Live memory of a trusted daemon just changed.

steps.title: Trigger
steps.caption: The attacker patches a function pointer inside the daemon and uses a short ptrace nudge to point the instruction register (RIP) at the new code. The daemon now runs attacker code.
